claims.text: Helm is a graduated Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) project.
A Helm chart is a directory of templated YAML manifests, a `values.yaml` file of default inputs, and metadata.
The `helm` CLI renders chart templates using Go template syntax and either installs the resulting manifests into a cluster as a release or prints them to stdout.
Helm charts are distributed through Helm repositories and indexed publicly on Artifact Hub.
Helm is open source under the Apache License 2.0 and the Helm project does not ship a commercial tier.
Pulumi supports authoring infrastructure in general-purpose languages (with loops, conditionals, classes, and package management), plus YAML and HCL.
In Pulumi, resource ordering is derived from the dependency graph: each resource waits for its dependencies to become ready, and independent resources deploy in parallel.
Helm applies resources in a fixed order by Kubernetes kind, defined in the kind_sorter.go file at helm/helm pkg/release/v1/util/kind_sorter.go.
Helm chart authors can't declare dependencies between resources or subcharts, except through hook weights.
The file pkg/release/v1/util/kind_sorter.go exists in the helm/helm repository main branch.
The Pulumi docs page /docs/iac/concepts/resources/options/dependson/ documents the dependency graph and the `dependsOn` resource option.
Pulumi's Automation API is a programmatic SDK in every supported Pulumi language for embedding `up`, `preview`, and `destroy` in a host application.
The Helm SDK is available in Go only; other languages must shell out to the `helm` CLI.
Pulumi Policies is open source, with rules written in Python, TypeScript, or Open Policy Agent Rego.
Pulumi Cloud adds centralized policy management on top of Pulumi Policies.
The Pulumi Enterprise edition adds Pulumi-maintained policy packs for CIS, PCI DSS, HITRUST, and NIST.
Helm has no native policy engine; policy is typically delegated to Kubernetes admission controllers such as Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper.
Pulumi is open source under the Apache License 2.0 (per the LICENSE file in pulumi/pulumi), and Helm is open source under the Apache License 2.0.
Helm doesn't let a chart author declare that one resource depends on another.
The Helm docs state: "the Kubernetes objects from the charts and all its dependencies are aggregated into a single set; then sorted by type followed by name; and then created/updated in that order."

Helm's install order is a hardcoded list of Kubernetes kinds in the Helm source, beginning with PriorityClasses and Namespaces, then Secrets and ConfigMaps, then CustomResourceDefinitions and RBAC, then Services and workloads, with any kind not on the list (including custom resources) last.
Helm uninstall runs the same kind-ordering list in reverse.
Helm sends the sorted manifests to the API server in a single pass and doesn't wait for one resource to become ready before applying the next.

Helm chart dependencies are a packaging mechanism and do not change resource ordering: a subchart's objects are merged into the parent chart's set and sorted by kind along with everything else (per the Helm docs' operational-aspects-of-using-dependencies section).
A Helm chart can't express 'install the database subchart before the application subchart' or 'start this Deployment after that Job completes.'
Helm chart hooks can be ordered with `helm.sh/hook-weight` annotations, and the resources created by hooks are not managed by Helm as part of the release.
Native sequencing for resources and subcharts in Helm has been proposed in HIP-0025, which is still a draft.
In Pulumi, passing one resource's output into another, or setting the `dependsOn` resource option, creates an edge in the dependency graph that determines operation order.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider waits for each resource to become ready before creating the resources that depend on it, and deploys independent resources in parallel.
Pulumi's parallel deployment of independent resources makes updates faster than a strict serial sequence.
Pulumi deletes resources following the dependency graph in reverse.

`helm.v4.Chart` in the Pulumi Kubernetes provider supports the `config.kubernetes.io/depends-on` annotation for ordering between objects inside the chart, and `dependsOn` on the chart resource for dependencies on resources outside it.

Helm manages Kubernetes resources only; a chart can install CRDs, workloads, services and other manifests into a cluster, but not resources outside the cluster such as a managed database, DNS record, or IAM role.
The Pulumi Registry covers AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, and SaaS platforms like Datadog, Auth0, GitHub, and Cloudflare.
Helm records each install or upgrade as a numbered release revision, and `helm rollback` restores a prior revision.
Pulumi runs through the local CLI, programmatically through the Automation API, or remotely through Pulumi Deployments.
A failed Pulumi update leaves the stack partially updated, and users roll forward by reverting program code and running `pulumi up`.
Helm favors fast revision-based rollback of a single release, while Pulumi favors scriptable control over resources from many providers in one update.
Helm and Pulumi are commonly used in combination rather than as substitutes.
Two patterns (cluster orchestration and wiring Pulumi outputs into chart values) cover most production deployments of Pulumi and Helm together.
A single Pulumi program can create an EKS, AKS, or GKE cluster, configure networking and IAM, and install cert-manager, ingress-nginx, and external-dns through `helm.v4.Chart` or `helm.v3.Release`.
The Pulumi EKS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/eks/ walks through the pattern of creating a cluster and installing the operational stack with Helm charts end-to-end.

Pulumi resource outputs (e.g., a database connection string from `aws.rds.Instance`, a KMS key ARN, a managed Redis endpoint, a Cloudflare zone ID) can flow into a Helm chart's `values` input as typed Pulumi outputs.
Pulumi resolves chart values at deploy time and orders/installs the chart after the resources it depends on.
The page contains an FAQ section 'What's the difference between `helm.Chart` and `helm.Release`?' that the anchor `#whats-the-difference-between-helmchart-and-helmrelease` resolves to.
Pulumi creates and deletes resources in dependency order, with each resource ready before the ones that depend on it, rather than in a fixed order by kind as Helm does.
There are three common ways to adopt Pulumi alongside or in place of Helm, which can be combined.
Using Helm charts directly from a Pulumi program with `helm.v4.Chart` or `helm.v3.Release` is the most common adoption pattern for Pulumi alongside Helm.
Charts can be converted to native Pulumi code by rendering them with `helm template` and converting the YAML with `pulumi convert --from kubernetes`.
`pulumi import` and the `import` resource option can import existing in-cluster resources and generate the corresponding code.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider exposes Helm charts as first-class resources through `helm.v4.Chart` and `helm.v3.Release`, and can pull charts from any Helm repository (public or private).

`helm.v4.Chart` renders chart templates locally and registers each Kubernetes object the chart produces as an individual Pulumi resource, so every child shows up in plan output, drift detection, and state.
`helm.v3.Release` uses the embedded Helm SDK and creates a real Helm release in the cluster, preserving chart hooks, post-rendering, and release history.

Helm merges the objects from a chart and all of its dependencies into a single set, sorts them by Kubernetes kind, and applies them in that order, so declaring a subchart as a dependency doesn't make it install first.
Ordering within a Helm release requires chart hooks with hook weights or logic in the application itself.

The page has sections 'Resource ordering and dependencies' and 'Adoption: coexistence, conversion, and import' matching the linked anchors #resource-ordering-and-dependencies and #adoption-coexistence-conversion-and-import.
The `values` input of Pulumi's Helm chart resources accepts the same shape as a `values.yaml` file but lets each leaf be a Pulumi output.
